extracted.intended_audience: scientists and educated general readers interested in logic and the scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for making ideas clear and for defining meaning, truth, and reality in scientific thought by focusing on practical effects, habits of action, and the method of investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief identity determined by mode of action
rubrics_metrics.description: If beliefs do not differ in the modes of action to which they give rise, then no mere differences in the manner of consciousness of them can make them different beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on what habits or rules of action a belief produces rather than differences in expression or the feeling of the belief; avoid drawing distinctions based only on manner of consciousness or expression (e.g., believing arrangement in Fig. 1 vs Fig. 2 may be the same belief if they produce the same action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mistaking subjective unclearness for an objective property
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mistake the sensation produced by our own unclearness of thought for a character of the object we are thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when obscurity is purely subjective; if a conception later appears in a clear form, we should not treat it as different merely because the feeling of unintelligibility is absent. Guard against this deception, especially on metaphysical ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't conflate grammatical differences with differences in ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere difference in the grammatical construction of two words is often mistaken for a distinction between the ideas they express.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to the idea's function and purpose rather than surface grammatical vagueness (example: saying 'thought is an action' vs 'it consists in a relation' involves grammatical vagueness but not necessarily inconsistency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of thought: produce habits of action (meaning-as-practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole function of thought is to produce habits of action; whatever is connected with a thought but irrelevant to its purpose is an accretion to it, but no part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To develop meaning, determine what habits a thought produces. What a thing means is simply what habits it involves; the identity of a habit depends on how it might lead us to act under possible circumstances, however improbable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third grade of clearness — define by conceivable practical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule for attaining the third grade of clearness of apprehension: consider what effects, which might conceivably have practical bearings, we conceive the object of our conception to have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Our conception of these effects is the whole of our conception of the object; analyze concepts by listing the sensible effects they would produce and how those effects would influence action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of qualities defined by conceived effects (illustrated by 'hard')
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole conception of a quality (e.g., calling a thing 'hard') lies in its conceived effects: that it will not be scratched by many other substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterfactuals about circumstances that do not actually arise are questions of arrangement of facts (language/usage), not of fact. Use such thought-experiments to sharpen logical principles but recognize when they only modify usage rather than meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reductio ad absurdum to test hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no objection to a contradiction in what would result from a false supposition; the reductio ad absurdum consists in showing that contradictory results would follow from a hypothesis which is consequently judged to be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply reductio to reveal falsehoods of hypotheses by deriving contradictions; this is a legitimate logical method for evaluating hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define scientific concepts by their practical explanatory role (example: Force)
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of Force represents that bodies in given relative positions always receive certain accelerations which, being compounded by geometrical addition, give the acceleration which the body actually experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand concepts by asking 'what is the immediate use of thinking about X?' and by representing the concept in terms of how it accounts for observable changes (e.g., represent accelerations by paths and compound them geometrically). Clarity requires grasping the fact the concept embodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the real (first formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The real is that whose characters are independent of what anybody may think them to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between figments (depend on someone's imagination) and external reality (characters independent of thought); recognize mental phenomena can be 'real' as occurrences in the mind without being real as external objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific conception of truth and reality (convergence criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion which is fated to be ultimately agreed to by all who investigate is what we mean by the truth, and the object represented in this opinion is the real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth is defined by the result of the scientific method carried sufficiently far: different methods may give differing initial results, but as methods are perfected results will move steadily together toward a destined centre. Reality/truth depend on what investigation, pushed far enough, would settle to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciliation of independence and investigatory dependence of reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reality is independent not necessarily of thought in general, but only of what you or I or any finite number of men may think; the object of the final opinion depends on what that opinion is, yet that opinion does not depend on what any finite set of men actually think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that while current or historical beliefs may delay settlement, the nature of the real is fixed by what sufficiently extended inquiry would produce; don't conflate temporary human perversity with ontological change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject methods of tenacity and authority in favor of investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of tenacity (fixing propositions arbitrarily) or authority (relying solely on tradition or scripture) do not ground the scientific idea of truth; scientific investigators believe investigation, if pushed far enough, will give one certain solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer methods that submit beliefs to inquiry and comparison of independent lines of evidence; beware loyalties that replace truth-seeking (historical examples: scholastic harmonizing of Aristotle and Church).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical significance overrides purely verbal arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about what would occur under circumstances which do not actually arise are not questions of fact but only of the most perspicuous arrangement of them; many such propositions concern the arrangement of our language more than the meaning of our ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing concepts, distinguish genuine substantive differences (practical effects on action) from mere linguistic or classificatory rearrangements; don't inflate importance of hypothetical scenarios that don't affect practice.
